theme: One level deeper — decompositions, hidden trade-offs and decision models

questions.concept: Anchoring a new habit to an existing user trigger
questions.question: You're the PM for a personal-finance app in India. Users who log expenses daily retain 3x better, but only 8% do it. Interviewer: 'Design a feature to get more users logging daily.' Which direction is strongest?
options: Prompt users to log right after a UPI payment notification, pre-filling the amount and merchant so logging takes one tap
Send a daily 9 PM push reminder to every user asking them to log the day's expenses
Add a streak counter and badges that reward users for logging seven days in a row
Run a campaign explaining why daily expense logging improves financial health
questions.explanation: Durable habits form when the new behaviour is attached to a trigger that already happens and the action is made nearly effortless. A UPI payment is a natural, frequent, in-context trigger, and pre-filling removes most of the work. Generic reminders, streaks and education add motivation but leave the effort and the context gap untouched.
rationales: Correct. It piggybacks on an existing, high-frequency event and cuts the action to one tap, addressing both trigger and ability.
A fixed-time reminder is an external trigger detached from the moment of spending; users must recall the whole day, so effort stays high and reminders get ignored.
Streaks can reinforce a habit that already exists, but they don't reduce the effort of logging and often punish lapses, causing drop-off.
Education raises motivation briefly but most users already know logging is good; the gap is effort and timing, not awareness.
questions.interview_tip: In product-sense rounds, link your solution to a behavioural mechanism (trigger, ability, motivation). Explaining why it works beats listing features.

questions.concept: Progressive disclosure for novice and power users
questions.question: A B2B invoicing SaaS has a settings page with 60 options. New SMB customers abandon setup, while enterprise admins demand even more controls. What design approach best serves both segments?
options: Show sensible defaults and the few essential settings up front, with advanced controls behind an expandable 'Advanced' section
Remove the 40 least-used settings to simplify the page for everyone
Build a separate enterprise-only product with its own settings page
Keep all 60 settings visible but add tooltips explaining each one
questions.explanation: Progressive disclosure shows the minimum needed for the common case and reveals complexity on demand. Novices get a short path with good defaults; power users still reach every control. It avoids both cutting needed features and forking the product.
rationales: Correct. Defaults plus layered advanced options lower cognitive load for SMBs without taking capability away from enterprise admins.
Deleting rarely used settings hurts the enterprise segment that relies on them; low usage doesn't mean low value.
Forking the product doubles maintenance and fragments the roadmap to solve what is a presentation problem.
Tooltips explain options but don't reduce the number of decisions; the overwhelm that drives abandonment remains.
questions.interview_tip: When two segments want opposite things, interviewers look for a solution that serves both rather than picking one blindly. Name the trade-off explicitly.

questions.concept: Empty state design to drive first action
questions.question: New users of a team task-management app land on an empty board and 45% never create a task. What is the most effective change to the empty state?
options: Pre-populate a sample project tied to the user's stated use case, with a clear prompt to create their first real task
Show a friendly illustration with the message 'No tasks yet'
Display a 10-minute video tour of all app features
Redirect new users to the settings page to configure their workspace first
questions.explanation: An empty state is onboarding real estate. A relevant template shows what 'good' looks like and a single clear call to action lowers the effort of the first step. Decorative messages, long tours and setup detours delay the moment of value.
rationales: Correct. A use-case template demonstrates value instantly and the prompt guides the user to the first meaningful action.
A friendly message is pleasant but gives no direction; the user still faces a blank page.
A long feature tour front-loads learning before value; most users skip or abandon it.
Configuration before any value adds friction at the riskiest moment of the journey.
questions.interview_tip: Onboarding questions test whether you think about time-to-value. Strong answers point to the first meaningful action and how to make it easy.

questions.question: You're designing a field app for FMCG sales reps visiting kirana stores in small Indian towns, where connectivity drops often. Reps complain orders get lost. What is the best product decision?
options: Make order capture work fully offline, store orders locally, and sync automatically with clear sync status when the network returns
Show an error and ask the rep to retry once they reach an area with better signal
Switch order capture to SMS so it works on 2G networks
Ask reps to note orders on paper and enter them in the app at the end of the day
questions.explanation: When the context of use guarantees bad connectivity, the core flow must not depend on the network. Offline-first capture with background sync and visible status prevents data loss and builds trust. The other options push the problem back onto the user or drop app value.
rationales: Correct. Local-first capture plus reliable sync solves the root problem, and visible status tells reps their work is safe.
Retry errors put the burden on the rep and still lose orders when they forget or never regain signal.
SMS works on weak networks but loses rich catalogs, validation and structure, and is error-prone for multi-line orders.
Paper doubles work and reintroduces transcription errors; it abandons the problem the app exists to solve.
questions.interview_tip: For emerging-market prompts, interviewers reward candidates who design for real constraints like connectivity, device and literacy rather than assuming ideal conditions.

questions.concept: Metric decomposition tree for a revenue drop
questions.question: A Shopify-based Indian D2C skincare brand sees weekly revenue drop 15% with no obvious cause. As PM, what should you do first?
options: Break revenue into sessions × conversion rate × average order value and find which component moved, then segment that one
Launch a 20% discount campaign to recover the lost revenue this week
Compare prices with the top three competitors to see if you've been undercut
Roll back the most recent website release as a precaution
questions.explanation: Decomposing the metric into its drivers localises the problem: a traffic drop points to marketing or SEO, a conversion drop to checkout or site issues, an AOV drop to mix or pricing. Then segment the moving component by channel, device or product. Acting before diagnosing risks treating the wrong cause.
rationales: Correct. A driver tree turns a vague drop into a specific, testable question about which lever changed.
Discounts may mask the symptom while burning margin, and they don't explain why revenue fell.
Competitor pricing is one hypothesis; jumping to it skips checking whether traffic or conversion even moved.
Rolling back without evidence may not help and costs whatever the release delivered; diagnose first.
questions.interview_tip: Root-cause questions reward structure. Say the decomposition out loud, then explain how each branch would point to a different team or fix.

questions.question: A support org sets a target to cut average handle time by 30%. Agents hit the target in a month, but customer satisfaction and repeat contacts get worse. What principle best explains this?
options: When a measure becomes a target, people optimise the measure itself and it stops reflecting the goal
Handle time is a lagging indicator, so it moved too slowly to be useful
The sample size was too small to detect the true effect on satisfaction
Customer satisfaction is a vanity metric and shouldn't be tracked
questions.explanation: Goodhart's law: targeting a proxy invites gaming. Agents shortened calls by rushing or transferring customers, which hit the number but hurt the real goal of resolving issues. Pair targets with counter-metrics and favour outcome measures like first-contact resolution.
rationales: Correct. This is Goodhart's law: the proxy was optimised at the expense of what it was meant to represent.
Handle time actually moved quickly; the problem is that it was gamed, not that it lagged.
Both metrics clearly moved; this isn't a statistical power issue but a behavioural response to the target.
Satisfaction tied to outcomes is meaningful here; it's what exposed the gaming.
questions.interview_tip: When you propose a target metric, interviewers often ask 'how could this be gamed?' Name the failure mode and your counter-metric before they ask.

questions.concept: Successful-search rate as a search quality metric
questions.question: You own search in a grocery delivery app. Which primary metric best captures whether search is working for users?
options: Share of searches that lead to a product being added to cart within the session
Total number of searches performed per day
Average number of results returned per query
Average time users spend on the search results page
questions.explanation: Search exists to help users find what they want. A successful-search rate (searches ending in an add-to-cart or click on a relevant item) measures that outcome. Raw query volume, result counts and dwell time can all rise when search is getting worse.
rationales: Correct. It ties search to the user's goal of finding and choosing a product.
More searches may mean users are reformulating because the first query failed.
More results isn't better; precise, relevant results matter more than volume.
Longer time on results often signals difficulty finding the item, not satisfaction.
questions.interview_tip: For 'define the metric' prompts, start from the user's job. Interviewers look for whether you can tell activity metrics from outcome metrics.

questions.concept: Compounding monthly churn into annual retention
questions.question: A subscription app has a steady 5% monthly churn among a cohort. Roughly what share of that cohort is still subscribed after 12 months?
options: About 54%
About 40%
About 46%
About 95%
questions.explanation: Churn compounds: each month 95% of the remaining users stay, so retention after 12 months is 0.95^12 ≈ 0.54. Simply multiplying 5% × 12 = 60% churned overstates loss because each month's churn applies to a shrinking base.
rationales: Correct. 0.95^12 ≈ 0.54, so about 54% remain.
This is the linear mistake (100% − 12 × 5%); churn applies to a shrinking base, so loss is smaller.
This is the share that churned (1 − 0.54), not the share retained.
95% is the one-month retention rate, not the 12-month figure.
questions.interview_tip: Quick compounding math shows up in SaaS and subscription cases. Doing it correctly and fast signals analytical comfort.

questions.concept: A/A test to validate the experiment platform
questions.question: Your team just built a new in-house experimentation platform. Before running real tests, what's the best way to check it isn't producing biased results?
options: Run A/A tests where both groups get the same experience and confirm significant differences appear only at about the expected false-positive rate
Run the most important planned feature test first and see if the results look sensible
Compare the platform's dashboard numbers with last quarter's business review
Ask a data scientist to review the platform's code
questions.explanation: In an A/A test there is no real difference, so roughly 5% of metrics should show significance at a 0.05 threshold. Many more indicates bugs in assignment, logging or variance calculations. It's the standard empirical check for a trustworthy platform.
rationales: Correct. A/A tests reveal bias and broken variance estimates because the true effect is known to be zero.
Using a real test as the check confuses platform bugs with treatment effects; 'sensible' results aren't proof.
Historical dashboards don't test randomisation or the statistics used to compare groups.
Code review helps but can miss data and logging issues that an A/A test exposes empirically.
questions.interview_tip: Mentioning A/A tests or sample-ratio checks when asked about trusting results signals real experimentation experience.

questions.concept: Post-hoc segment slicing of a flat test
questions.question: A checkout redesign A/B test shows no overall effect. An analyst slices the results into 20 segments and finds that iOS users in Tier-2 cities improved conversion by 6% (p = 0.03). The team wants to ship to that segment. What do you do?
options: Treat it as a hypothesis and run a new test targeted at that segment before shipping
Ship to that segment now since p = 0.03 is below the 0.05 threshold
Ship to everyone because one segment improved and the others didn't get worse
Discard the finding entirely because segment analysis is always invalid
questions.explanation: Checking 20 segments at α = 0.05 gives about a 64% chance of at least one false positive. A post-hoc hit is a lead, not a conclusion. Confirm it with a pre-registered test on that segment, ideally with a plausible mechanism.
rationales: Correct. Re-testing turns a likely multiple-comparisons artifact into a real, confirmable finding.
The p-value isn't valid on its own after 20 looks; the chance of a spurious winner is high.
The overall result was flat; shipping broadly on one noisy segment ignores the main readout.
Segment analysis is useful for generating hypotheses; the error is treating it as confirmation.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers love the 'we found a winning segment' trap. Naming multiple comparisons and proposing a confirmatory test is the strong answer.

questions.concept: Daily consumption estimate for a city
questions.question: Estimate the number of cups of tea consumed per day in Bengaluru (at home and outside). Assume about 14 million residents.
options: About 14 million
About 1.4 million
About 140 million
About 1.4 billion
questions.explanation: Method: 14M people × ~50% who drink tea (coffee is popular in Bengaluru, and young children don't drink tea) × ~2 cups a day ≈ 14M cups. Reasonable alternative assumptions land between ~8M and ~20M, so 14 million is the right order of magnitude.
rationales: Correct. Population × share of tea drinkers × cups per drinker gives roughly 14 million.
This implies only 1 in 10 people drinks one cup a day, far too low for an Indian city.
This needs every resident to drink 10 cups daily, which is implausible.
This exceeds 100 cups per person per day, an order-of-magnitude error.
questions.interview_tip: Estimation rounds grade the method more than the number. State the segmentation and assumptions, then sanity-check the result per person.

questions.concept: Fleet size from peak demand and rider throughput
questions.question: A quick-commerce app expects 20,000 orders in its busiest hour in one city. Each delivery round trip takes about 24 minutes, and you want a 20% buffer for idle time and breaks. Roughly how many riders do you need on shift at peak?
options: About 10,000
About 1,000
About 20,000
About 50,000
questions.explanation: Each rider completes 60 / 24 = 2.5 deliveries an hour. 20,000 / 2.5 = 8,000 riders, plus a 20% buffer ≈ 9,600, so about 10,000. Sizing to peak hour (not daily average) is what matters for capacity.
rationales: This would need each rider to do 20 deliveries an hour, impossible with 24-minute trips.
This assumes one rider per order, ignoring that riders complete multiple trips per hour.
This overestimates by 5x, as if each delivery took about two hours.
questions.interview_tip: Capacity estimates come up in marketplace and logistics loops. Showing throughput per unit and adding a buffer signals operational thinking.

questions.question: A water-purifier company sells its RO units close to cost but earns most of its profit from proprietary replacement filters and service plans. Which business model is this?
options: Razor-and-blades
Freemium
Marketplace take rate
Usage-based SaaS pricing
questions.explanation: Razor-and-blades sells the base product cheaply to build an installed base, then profits from recurring, often proprietary consumables. It works when consumables are needed regularly and hard to substitute.
rationales: Correct. A cheap base unit plus high-margin recurring consumables is the classic razor-and-blades model.
Freemium gives a basic version free and upsells premium features; here the hardware is sold, not given free.
A take rate is a commission on transactions between third parties, which isn't happening here.
Usage-based SaaS charges for software consumption, not physical consumables tied to hardware.
questions.interview_tip: Naming the model is the start; strong candidates also explain what makes it defensible, here lock-in to proprietary consumables.

questions.concept: Build vs buy vs partner decision
questions.question: Your B2B HR platform needs payroll compliance across 15 Indian states within six months to win enterprise deals. It isn't your core differentiator, and a mature payroll provider offers an API. What is the best call?
options: Partner and integrate the provider's API, owning the user experience while keeping your engineers on your core differentiators
Build payroll in-house so you control the full stack from day one
Acquire a small payroll startup to own the capability outright
Wait until enough customers ask for it before deciding anything
questions.explanation: Build what differentiates you; partner or buy what doesn't, especially when time-to-market matters and a mature option exists. Integrating keeps the experience yours while avoiding years of compliance work. An acquisition is costly and slow for a non-core need.
rationales: Correct. A non-core capability, a tight deadline and a mature API point to partnering.
Building complex compliance in-house consumes scarce engineering on a non-differentiator and likely misses the six-month window.
Acquisition is expensive, slow to integrate and overkill when an API partnership meets the need.
Enterprise deals already depend on it; waiting means losing the deals that create the demand signal.
questions.interview_tip: Build/buy/partner questions test judgment. Use explicit criteria like differentiation, time-to-market, cost and control, then make a call.

questions.question: A SaaS company offers Basic at ₹500 and Pro at ₹1,200 per month, and most users choose Basic. It adds a 'Plus' tier at ₹1,100 with clearly fewer features than Pro, and Pro sign-ups rise. What explains this?
options: The decoy effect: an inferior option priced close to Pro makes Pro look like the obvious value
Price anchoring to the lowest tier made Basic look cheaper
Users prefer more choices, so adding any tier increases conversion
Plus cannibalised Basic, pushing users toward the top tier
questions.explanation: An asymmetrically dominated option (Plus) is worse than Pro at nearly the same price, so it makes Pro look like a bargain by comparison. The decoy itself is not meant to sell; its job is to shift choice toward the target tier.
rationales: Correct. Plus is dominated by Pro, which nudges users to see Pro as the best deal.
Anchoring on the lowest tier would make Basic more attractive, the opposite of what happened.
More choice often reduces conversion (choice overload); the specific dominated design is what worked here.
Plus didn't take Basic users; it changed how Pro was perceived relative to its neighbour.
questions.interview_tip: Pricing questions reward understanding of buyer psychology. Mention the ethics of decoys and that real value should back the target tier.

questions.question: A feature built two years ago is used by 2% of users, causes 15% of support tickets and slows every release. A few vocal customers love it. What's the best way to handle it?
options: Check who those users are and their value, then plan a deprecation with notice, a migration path and a clear timeline
Remove it in the next release since only 2% of users rely on it
Keep it indefinitely because removing features upsets customers
Hide it from new users but keep maintaining it for existing users forever
questions.explanation: Sunsetting is a product decision about total cost (support, complexity, velocity) versus value to the users who depend on it. Understand who those 2% are (they could be top accounts), then deprecate with communication and alternatives to protect trust.
rationales: Correct. It weighs real costs against the affected users' value and protects trust with a planned migration.
Abrupt removal can hit high-value accounts and damage trust; 2% of users may be a large share of revenue.
Keeping everything forever compounds complexity and slows the whole team.
Hiding it keeps all the maintenance and support costs while still limiting future value.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like 'what would you kill?' questions. Good answers quantify the cost of keeping a feature and show care in how you remove it.

questions.question: Which acceptance criterion is written so engineering and QA can verify it unambiguously?
options: Given a logged-in user with items in cart, when they apply an expired coupon, then an 'expired coupon' message appears and the total is unchanged
Coupons should work correctly and show clear messages to the user
The coupon flow should be fast, intuitive and delightful for customers
Handle all edge cases for coupons as discussed in the planning meeting
questions.explanation: Given-When-Then states the precondition, the action and the observable outcome, so the criterion is testable. Vague words like 'correctly', 'intuitive' or 'as discussed' can't be verified and lead to rework.
rationales: Correct. It names the context, trigger and expected result, which makes it directly testable.
'Work correctly' and 'clear' are subjective and can't be checked objectively.
'Fast' and 'delightful' have no thresholds, so pass or fail is a matter of opinion.
It points to an undocumented conversation instead of stating the expected behaviour.
questions.interview_tip: Execution interviews may ask how you write specs. Showing testable criteria signals that you reduce ambiguity for engineering.

questions.concept: Dark launch to test backend load
questions.question: You're launching a new recommendations service that will receive millions of requests a day. You want to see how it performs under real production load before any user sees its output. What should you do?
options: Dark launch it: send real traffic to the new service in the background without showing its results to users
Run a 50/50 A/B test so half of users see the new recommendations
Load-test only in staging with synthetic traffic, then launch to 100%
Launch to internal employees for a week before rolling out
questions.explanation: A dark launch exercises the new system with real production traffic while users still see the old experience. It surfaces load, latency and error issues without user impact. User-facing tests come after the system is proven stable.
rationales: Correct. Shadow traffic tests real load safely because users never see the new output.
An A/B test exposes users to a system that hasn't been proven under load; failures would hurt half the users.
Synthetic staging traffic rarely matches real production patterns, so issues can still appear at launch.
Employee traffic is far too small to reveal behaviour at millions of requests a day.
questions.interview_tip: Launch-planning answers stand out when you separate system risk (load, errors) from product risk (user impact) and match a technique to each.

questions.question: In a leadership review, a peer PM presents a cross-team analysis that was mostly your team's work and doesn't mention your team. How should you handle it?
options: Talk to the peer privately, assume good intent, explain the impact on your team, and agree how to credit shared work going forward
Interrupt the review to clarify that your team did most of the work
Email the leadership group afterwards listing your team's contributions
Say nothing to keep the relationship smooth and move on
questions.explanation: A strong response protects the team's recognition and the working relationship. A private, direct conversation that focuses on impact and a forward-looking agreement resolves the issue without public conflict. Silence lets it repeat, and public escalation damages trust.
rationales: Correct. It's direct, private, assumes good intent and sets a norm that prevents repeats.
Correcting a peer publicly in a leadership review looks defensive and hurts collaboration.
Going over the peer's head before talking to them escalates prematurely and reads as political.
Avoiding the conversation lets your team go unrecognised and the behaviour continue.
questions.interview_tip: Conflict questions test maturity. Interviewers look for directness, empathy, care for your team, and a concrete resolution.

questions.concept: When customer anecdotes contradict the metrics
questions.question: Your dashboard shows average delivery-time promises are met 98% of the time, yet several customers and a senior leader report frequent late deliveries. In an Amazon-style interview, what's the best response to describe?
options: Treat the anecdotes as a signal the measurement may be wrong, dig into how the metric is computed, and find the gap
Trust the dashboard, since 98% is based on all orders and anecdotes are a biased sample
Apologise to the complaining customers and offer them credits
Commission a customer survey next quarter to settle the disagreement
questions.explanation: When anecdotes and data disagree, the anecdotes are often pointing to a flaw in how something is measured, for example a metric based on the promise date shown after a silent extension, or one that excludes certain regions. Diving deep into the metric definition is the Customer Obsession and Dive Deep move.
rationales: Correct. It uses the anecdotes to audit the metric itself, which is where the truth often hides.
Dismissing customer reports defends the dashboard rather than the customer; the metric may not measure what customers experience.
Credits treat the symptom for a few people but leave the underlying problem undiscovered.
Waiting a quarter is slow; you can check the metric's definition and raw data now.
questions.interview_tip: Amazon interviewers probe Dive Deep and Customer Obsession. Stories where you found a flaw in a trusted metric are especially strong.

questions.question: A senior engineer on your team often dismisses design feedback in reviews, and the designer has stopped speaking up. What's the best way to give the engineer feedback?
options: In private, describe a specific recent meeting, the behaviour you saw, and its impact on the designer and the product, then ask for their view
Tell them in the next team meeting that everyone should be more respectful
Ask their engineering manager to handle it so you don't hurt your relationship
Wait for the performance review cycle to raise it formally
questions.explanation: Situation-behaviour-impact keeps feedback specific, factual and non-judgmental, and asking for their view opens a dialogue. Doing it privately and promptly makes it actionable. Vague group comments, outsourcing it, or delay all reduce the chance of change.
rationales: Correct. Specific, private and timely feedback focused on impact is most likely to change behaviour.
A vague group message doesn't reach the person and may embarrass others; the issue stays unresolved.
Escalating before talking directly avoids ownership and can feel like going behind their back.
Waiting months lets the harm continue and makes the feedback feel like an ambush.
questions.interview_tip: Leadership-without-authority questions often involve feedback to peers. Use a named framework and show you followed up.

questions.concept: Pinning model versions to avoid silent behaviour changes
questions.question: Your app calls an LLM API through a 'latest' model alias. One morning, output formatting changes and your parser breaks, though you shipped nothing. What should you do to prevent this?
options: Pin a specific model version and upgrade deliberately after running your eval suite on the new version
Switch to a different LLM vendor whose models never change
Add more instructions to the prompt telling the model never to change its format
Turn temperature down to 0 so outputs stay consistent across updates
questions.explanation: A 'latest' alias can point to a new model at any time, changing behaviour without a release on your side. Pinning a dated version and upgrading through evals makes model changes a controlled release.
rationales: Correct. Version pinning plus an eval gate turns surprise changes into planned upgrades.
All vendors update and retire models; switching vendors doesn't remove the risk.
Prompt instructions can't stop the underlying model being swapped, and new models may follow them differently.
Temperature affects randomness within one model, not changes caused by a different model behind the alias.
questions.interview_tip: AI PM interviews increasingly test operational maturity. Treating model upgrades like releases with evals is a strong signal.

questions.question: You're shipping an AI agent that books travel for employees. The team proposes evaluating it on how closely each step matches a reference sequence of tool calls. What's the main problem with that as the primary eval?
options: Many valid paths reach the same goal, so the primary measure should be whether the task was completed correctly within policy
Tool-call matching is too expensive to run in CI
Reference sequences can't be written for travel booking
Step matching only works with open-source models
questions.explanation: Agents can solve a task in different orders or with different tools. Penalising valid alternative paths gives misleading scores. Make end-state correctness (right booking, within policy and budget) primary, and use trajectory checks as secondary diagnostics for cost, safety and loops.
rationales: Correct. Outcome checks reward what users care about; trajectory matching wrongly penalises valid paths.
Matching tool calls is cheap to compute; cost isn't the core issue.
Reference sequences can be written; the problem is that they aren't the only correct path.
Step matching is model-agnostic; it applies equally to open and closed models.
questions.interview_tip: When discussing agents, distinguish outcome metrics from process metrics. Interviewers want to see you'd measure what users actually value.

questions.question: A RAG assistant for an electronics retailer handles 'laptop good for travel' well but fails on exact queries like 'SKU LX-4471B'. What's the best fix?
options: Combine keyword (lexical) search with vector search so exact identifiers and semantic meaning are both matched
Increase the number of retrieved chunks from 5 to 50
Switch to a larger LLM so it can infer the right SKU
Fine-tune the embedding model on product descriptions
questions.explanation: Dense embeddings capture meaning but handle rare, exact tokens like SKUs and codes poorly. Lexical search such as BM25 excels at exact matches. Hybrid retrieval merges both result sets.
rationales: Correct. Hybrid search covers exact identifiers and semantic intent together.
Pulling more chunks adds noise and cost; the right SKU may still not be retrieved by semantic similarity.
The generator can't use a document that wasn't retrieved; this is a retrieval problem.
Fine-tuning embeddings on descriptions doesn't make arbitrary codes semantically matchable and is costly.
questions.interview_tip: Showing you know where retrieval fails (exact codes, names, numbers) signals hands-on RAG experience.

questions.question: An LLM classifying customer emails into five categories keeps mixing up 'billing' and 'refund'. What's the quickest prompt change most likely to help?
options: Add a few labelled examples, including ones that show the difference between billing and refund emails
Ask the model to be more careful and accurate
Raise the temperature to encourage more varied answers
Make the system prompt longer by describing the company's history
questions.explanation: Few-shot prompting shows the model concrete input-output pairs, which is especially effective at clarifying boundaries between similar classes. It's cheap and fast to try before fine-tuning.
rationales: Correct. Targeted examples teach the model where the boundary between confusable classes lies.
Generic exhortations rarely change behaviour; the model needs information, not encouragement.
Higher temperature adds randomness, which hurts consistency in classification.
Irrelevant context adds tokens and cost without clarifying the category boundary.
questions.interview_tip: Interviewers like to see a cheapest-first ladder: prompt and examples, then retrieval, then fine-tuning.

questions.question: Your product uses a large frontier model for a narrow task: extracting fields from invoices. Quality is great but cost and latency are too high at scale. What's a strong option?
options: Use the large model's outputs on many invoices to fine-tune a small model for this task, then verify it matches quality on your evals
Shorten the invoices by truncating them to the first 500 tokens
Batch all invoices once a day to get a volume discount
Keep the large model and raise prices to cover the cost
questions.explanation: Distillation transfers a narrow capability from a large 'teacher' to a small 'student', often keeping most of the quality at a fraction of the cost and latency. Evals confirm the student is good enough before switching.
rationales: Correct. A distilled small model fits narrow, high-volume tasks well, and evals guard quality.
Truncation can cut off fields like totals that appear later, hurting accuracy.
Batch discounts reduce cost but increase latency, and users may need results quickly.
Raising prices pushes the cost to customers instead of fixing an inefficient architecture.
questions.interview_tip: Cost questions in AI PM loops reward a menu of levers: routing, caching, distillation, and their quality trade-offs.

questions.question: Your app needs to know when a payment succeeds at the payment gateway. What's the main advantage of webhooks over repeatedly polling the gateway's API?
options: The gateway pushes an event when the payment status changes, so you learn quickly without making wasteful repeated requests
Webhooks guarantee every event arrives exactly once
Webhooks don't need any authentication or signature checks
Polling can't be used with payment gateways
questions.explanation: With webhooks, the provider calls your endpoint when something happens, giving near-real-time updates without constant requests. Webhooks can still be delayed or duplicated, so handlers must verify signatures and be idempotent.
rationales: Correct. Push-based events are timely and avoid the cost and rate-limit pressure of polling.
Webhooks are usually delivered at least once, so duplicates can happen; you must handle them.
Webhook endpoints must verify signatures, or anyone could send fake payment events.
Polling works with gateways; it's just less efficient and slower to react.
questions.interview_tip: Technical-fluency questions check you understand integration trade-offs well enough to discuss them with engineers.

questions.question: Traffic to your web service is growing 10x over the next year. Engineering proposes adding more servers behind a load balancer rather than buying a bigger single server. What's the main reason?
options: Horizontal scaling adds capacity almost without limit and removes the single point of failure
Bigger servers are always more expensive per request than many small ones
Horizontal scaling requires no changes to the application
Vertical scaling makes the database slower
questions.explanation: Vertical scaling hits hardware ceilings and leaves one machine as a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling spreads load across many nodes for higher ceilings and resilience, though it usually needs stateless services and more operational complexity.
rationales: Correct. More nodes give near-unlimited headroom and resilience if one fails.
Cost per request varies; the key advantages are headroom and fault tolerance, not guaranteed cheapness.
Horizontal scaling often requires changes, such as moving session state out of servers.
A bigger machine doesn't slow the database; this misstates the trade-off.
questions.interview_tip: You won't design systems in PM loops, but explaining why a scaling choice matters for reliability and cost earns engineering credibility.

questions.question: A fintech app's referral program gives ₹100 to the referrer only. Shares are high but few invitees sign up. What change is most likely to improve conversion?
options: Give the invitee a reward too, triggered when they complete a meaningful action such as a first transaction
Double the referrer's reward to ₹200
Let users share the invite on more social channels
Remove the reward and rely on users' goodwill
questions.explanation: The bottleneck is invitee conversion, not sharing. A two-sided reward gives invitees a reason to act, and tying it to a meaningful action ensures you pay for quality users rather than empty sign-ups.
rationales: Correct. It targets the weak step (invitee conversion) and links the payout to real value.
A bigger referrer reward boosts sharing, which is already high, and can encourage spam.
More channels increase reach but don't give the invitee any reason to convert.
Removing incentives would likely reduce both sharing and conversion.
questions.interview_tip: Growth answers are strongest when you identify the exact funnel step that's leaking before choosing a lever.

questions.question: On 1 October 2026 Cloudflare introduced Clef and Clef-flash on Workers AI as 'decision models'. According to Cloudflare, what do these models return, in contrast with general-purpose LLMs?
options: Typed answers with probabilities, for decisions such as routing or escalating a support ticket
Long-form text with inline citations for research questions
Generated images and video for marketing content
Full multi-step plans that execute tool calls automatically
questions.explanation: Cloudflare's post says 'a decision model will return typed answers with probabilities', for classification and routing inside agent workflows, such as support triage, escalation or threat classification. Both are released under Apache 2.0, and Clef-flash is pitched for latency-critical decisions. For PMs, probability outputs make confidence thresholds and routing to humans easier to design.
rationales: Correct. Cloudflare describes them as returning strictly typed answers with probabilities for agents to act on.
Open-ended text generation is what Cloudflare contrasts decision models against.
They're classification models, not image or video generators.
They help agents decide how to act, but generating tool calls is the open-ended LLM role Cloudflare contrasts them with.
questions.interview_tip: On a 'what do you think of this launch?' question, explain the job it does (cheap, structured decisions inside agents) and how it changes product design, for example confidence-based routing.
